entries.4d288c402879b8946fe5a02de05b8c0945007b14: <div sID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="1Chr.19" sID="1Chr.19"/> <div eID="gen7838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7839" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> The story is here repeated of David's war with the Ammonites and the Syrians their allies, and the victories he obtained over them, which we read just as it is here related, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.19">2 Sam. x.</reference> Here is, I. David's civility to the king of Ammon, in sending an embassy of condolence to him on occasion of his father's death, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1-1Chr.19.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His great incivility to David, in the base usage he gave to his ambassadors, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.3-1Chr.19.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. David's just resentment of it, and the war which broke out thereupon, in which the Ammonites acted with policy in bringing the Syrians to their assistance (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6-1Chr.19.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>), Joab did bravely (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.8-1Chr.19.13">ver. 8-13</reference>), and Israel was once and again victorious, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.14-1Chr.19.19">ver. 14-19</reference>.
entries.4bf4e25214bdb98894aa32621c37a1f6c6605345: <div eID="gen7840" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7839" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ill Usage of David's Servants. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1037.)</title> <div sID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died, and his son reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David said, I will shew kindness unto Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me. And David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. So the servants of David came into the land of the children of Ammon to Hanun, to comfort him. <hi type="super">3</hi> But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father, that he hath sent comforters unto thee? are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spy out the land? <hi type="super">4</hi> Wherefore Hanun took David's servants, and shaved them, and cut off their garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then there went <hi type="italic">certain,</hi> and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them: for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, Tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and <hi type="italic">then</hi> return. <div eID="gen7841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> Let us here observe, 1. That is becomes good people to be neighbourly, and especially to be grateful. David will pay respect to Hanun because he is his neighbour; and religion teaches us to be civil and obliging to all, to honour all men, and to be ready to do all offices of kindness to those we live among; nor must difference in religion be any obstruction to this. But, besides this, David remembered the kindness which his father showed to him. Those that have received kindness must return it as they have ability and opportunity: those that have received it from the parents must return it to the children when they are gone. 2. That, as saith the proverb of the ancients, <hi type="italic">Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>. The vile person will speak villany, and the instruments of the churl will be evil, to <hi type="italic">destroy those with lying words that speak right,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6-Isa.32.7">Isa. xxxii. 6, 7</reference>. Those that are base, and design ill themselves, are apt to be jealous and to suspect ill of others without cause. Hanun's servant suggested that David's ambassadors came as spies, as if so great and mighty a man as David needed to do so mean a thing (if he had any design upon the Ammonites, he could effect it by open force, and had no occasion for any fraudulent practices), or as if a man of such virtue and honour would do so base a thing. Yet Hanun hearkened to the suggestion, and, against the law of nations, treated David's ambassadors villainously. 3. Masters ought to protect their servants, and with the greatest tenderness to concern themselves for them if they come by any loss or damage in their service. David did so for his ambassadors, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.5">v. 5</reference>. Christ will do so for his ministers; and let all masters thus <hi type="italic">give unto their servants that which is just and equal.</hi>
entries.79fe636a74b7381a2cd1bfdd657b87b1a53b4c61: <div eID="gen7842" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Defeat of the Ammonites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1036.)</title> <div sID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syria-maachah, and out of Zobah. <hi type="super">7</hi> So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots, and the king of Maachah and his people; who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battle. <hi type="super">8</hi> And when David heard <hi type="italic">of it,</hi> he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men. <hi type="super">9</hi> And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battle in array before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come <hi type="italic">were</hi> by themselves in the field. <hi type="super">10</hi> Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice of Israel, and put <hi type="italic">them</hi> in array against the Syrians. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of Abishai his brother, and they set <hi type="italic">themselves</hi> in array against the children of Ammon. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he said, If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee. <hi type="super">13</hi> Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> do <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> good in his sight. <hi type="super">14</hi> So Joab and the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him drew nigh before the Syrians unto the battle; and they fled before him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother, and entered into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers, and drew forth the Syrians that <hi type="italic">were</hi> beyond the river: and Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer <hi type="italic">went</hi> before them. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it was told David; and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set <hi type="italic">the battle</hi> in array against them. So when David had put the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him. <hi type="super">18</hi> But the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand <hi type="italic">men which fought in</hi> chariots, and forty thousand footmen, and killed Shophach the captain of the host. <hi type="super">19</hi> And when the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David, and became his servants: neither would the Syrians help the children of Ammon any more. <div eID="gen7843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7844" type="x-p"/> We may see here, 1. How the hearts of sinners that are marked for ruin are hardened to their destruction. The children of Ammon saw that <hi type="italic">they had made themselves odious to David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">v. 6</reference>), and then it would have been their wisdom to desire conditions of peace, to humble themselves and offer any satisfaction for the injury they had done him, the rather because they had made themselves not only odious to David, but obnoxious to the justice of God, who is <hi type="italic">King of nations,</hi> and will assert the injured rights and maintain the violated laws of nations. But, instead of this, they prepared for war, and so brought upon themselves, by David's hand, those desolations which he never intended them. 2. How the courage of brave men is heightened and invigorated by difficulties. When Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.10">v. 10</reference>), instead of meditating a retreat, he doubled his resolution; and, though he could not double, he divided his army, and not only spoke, but acted, like a gallant man, that had great presence of mind when he saw himself surrounded. He engaged with his brother for mutual assistance (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.12">v. 12</reference>), excited himself and the rest of the officers to act vigorously in their respective posts, with an eye to God's glory and their country's good, not to any honour and advantage of their own, and then left the issue to God: <hi type="italic">Let the Lord do that which is right in his sight.</hi> 3. How vain the greatest art and strength are against justice and equity. The Ammonites did their utmost to make the best of their position: they brought as good a force into the field, and disposed it with as much policy as possible; yet, having a bad cause, and acting in defence of wrong, it would not do; they were put to the worst. Right will prevail and triumph at last. 4. To how little purpose it is for those to rally again, and reinforce themselves, that have not God on their side. The Syrians, though in no way concerned in the merits of the cause, but serving only as mercenaries to the Ammonites, when they were beaten, thought themselves concerned to retrieve their honour, and therefore called in the assistance of the Syrians on the other side Euphrates; but to no purpose, for still they <hi type="italic">fled before Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.18">v. 18</reference>); they lost 7000 men, who are said to be the men of 700 chariots, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2 Sam. x. 18</reference>. For, as now in a man of war for sea-service they allot ten men to a gun, so then, in land-service, ten men to a chariot. 5. those who have <hi type="italic">meddled with strife that belongs not to them,</hi> and have found that they <hi type="italic">meddled to their own heart,</hi> do well to learn wit at length and meddle no further. The Syrians, finding that Israel was the conquering side, not only broke off their alliance with the Ammonites and would help them no more (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">but made peace with David and became his servants.</hi> Let those who have in vain stood it out against God be thus wise for themselves, and <hi type="italic">agree with him quickly, while they are in the way.</hi> Let them become his servants; for they cannot but see themselves undone if they be his enemies.  <chapter eID="1Chr.19"/> <div eID="gen7844" type="x-p"/>

entries.e723f6ced7b607f75792fc2b580d3b9242530991: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3810"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 19</title> <div sID="gen5465" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1-1Chr.19.5">1Ch 19:1-5</reference>. David's Messengers, Sent to Comfort Hanun, Are Disgracefully Treated.<div eID="gen5465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3810"/><hi type="bold">1. after this--</hi>This phrase seems to indicate that the incident now to be related took place immediately, or soon after the wars described in the preceding chapter. But the chronological order is loosely observed, and the only just inference that can be drawn from the use of this phrase is, that some farther account is to be given of the wars against the Syrians.<div eID="gen5466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died--</hi>There had subsisted a very friendly relation between David and him, begun during the exile of the former, and cemented, doubtless, by their common hostility to Saul. <div eID="gen5467" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f392fec19169fda20d1e41ebeb00e78266da14f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3811"/><div sID="gen5468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3811"/><hi type="bold">3. are not his servants come unto thee for to search?--</hi>that is, thy capital, Rabbah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sa 10:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5468" type="x-p"/>
entries.967260bf10a5fba8b40a89ee34e029eefae2db6f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3812"/><div sID="gen5469" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3812"/><hi type="bold">4-5. shaved them--</hi>not completely, but only the half of their face. This disrespect to the beard, and indecent exposure of their persons by their clothes being cut off from the girdle downwards, was the grossest indignity to which Jews, in common with all Orientals, could be subjected. No wonder that the men were ashamed to appear in public--that the king recommended them to remain in seclusion on the border till the mark of their disgrace had disappeared--and then they might, with propriety, return to the court.<div eID="gen5469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5470" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6-1Chr.19.15">1Ch 19:6-15</reference>. Joab and Abishai Overcome the Ammonites. <div eID="gen5470" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e672658525d5c914e3db0cd2cf3051de6939a34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3813"/><div sID="gen5471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3813"/><hi type="bold">6. when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David--</hi>One universal feeling of indignation was roused throughout Israel, and all classes supported the king in his determination to avenge this unprovoked insult on the Hebrew nation.<div eID="gen5471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hanun ... sent a thousand talents of silver--</hi>a sum equal to £342,100, to procure the services of foreign mercenaries.<div eID="gen5472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia ... Syria-maachah, and ... Zobah--</hi>The Mesopotamian troops did not arrive during this campaign (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.16">1Ch 19:16</reference>). Syria-maachah lay on the north of the possessions of the trans-jordanic Israelites, near Gilead.<div eID="gen5473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5474" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zobah--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.18.3">1Ch 18:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5474" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e589552a8029345650f90de8d0308ae7c32270d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3814"/><div sID="gen5475" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3814"/><hi type="bold">7. So they hired thirty and two thousand chariots--</hi>Hebrew, "riders," or "cavalry," accustomed to fight either on horseback or in chariots, and occasionally on foot. Accepting this as the true rendering, the number of hired auxiliaries mentioned in this passage agrees exactly with the statement in <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.6">2Sa 10:6</reference>: twenty thousand (from Syria), twelve thousand (from Tob), equal to thirty-two thousand, and one thousand with the king of Maachah. <div eID="gen5475" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4191b1237d3a6de7fd7570c66f719dac4d8440f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3815"/><div sID="gen5476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3815"/><hi type="bold">8. David ... sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty men--</hi>All the forces of Israel, including the great military orders, were engaged in this war. <div eID="gen5476" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc57d976a679c3a14b1082c76ba12fc4eb165dfd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3816"/><div sID="gen5477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3816"/><hi type="bold">9-15. children of Ammon ... put the battle in array before the gate of the city--</hi>that is, outside the walls of Medeba, a frontier town on the Arnon.<div eID="gen5477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5478" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kings that were come were by themselves in the field--</hi>The Israelitish army being thus beset by the Ammonites in front, and by the Syrian auxiliaries behind, Joab resolved to attack the latter (the more numerous and formidable host), while he directed his brother Abishai, with a suitable detachment, to attack the Ammonites. Joab's address before the engagement displays the faith and piety that became a commander of the Hebrew people. The mercenaries being defeated, the courage of the Ammonites failed; so that, taking flight, they entrenched themselves within the fortified walls.<div eID="gen5478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5479" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.16-1Chr.19.19">1Ch 19:16-19</reference>. Shophach Slain by David. <div eID="gen5479" type="x-p"/>
entries.30a50db5462829ed928c6623b834822810de1de7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3817"/><div sID="gen5480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3817"/><hi type="bold">16. And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.15-2Sam.10.19">2Sa 10:15-19</reference>). <div eID="gen5480" type="x-p"/>
entries.53c3d4e9798428b2a34ed0890537d97ad6a319f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3818"/><div sID="gen5481" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3818"/><hi type="bold">18. David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sa 10:18</reference>, which has seven hundred chariots). Either the text in one of the books is corrupt [Keil, Davidson], or the accounts must be combined, giving this result--seven thousand horsemen, seven thousand chariots, and forty thousand footmen [Kennicott, Houbigant, Calmet]. <chapter eID="1Chr.19"/>

entries.35689716b49eca8187a64e6bc8b11e92904658a8: <div eID="gen13689" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13690" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13691" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13690" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> David sends a congratulatory message to Hanun, king of Ammon, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1">1Chr 19:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.2">1Chr 19:2</reference>. He treats the messengers with great incivility, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.3">1Chr 19:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.4">1Chr 19:4</reference>. David is exasperated, but condoles with the degraded messengers, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.5">1Chr 19:5</reference>. The Ammonites prepare for war, and hire thirty-two thousand chariots, and besiege Medeba, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">1Chr 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Chr 19:7</reference>. David sends Joab to attack them; he defeats the Syrians and Ammonites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.8-1Chr.19.15">1Chr 19:8-15</reference>. The discomfited Syrians recruit their army, and invade David's territories beyond Jordan; he attacks them, kills Shophach their general, seven thousand charioteers, and forty thousand of their infantry, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.16-1Chr.19.18">1Chr 19:16-18</reference>. The Syrians abandon the Ammonites and make a separate peace with David, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.19">1Chr 19:19</reference>. <div eID="gen13692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> Now it came to pass - See the same history, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sam 10:1</reference> (note), etc., and the notes there.
entries.c23dbcdfe59da1055ac170197843cc3cd0191708: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen13694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> And cut off their garments in the midst - Usque ad eorum, pudenda. So the Targum, Jarchi, and others; leaving exposed what nature and decency require to be concealed. See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference> (note).
entries.4992b9470acb0a5bb091e446d0b0fcf7b3ffc553: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen13695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> Chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia - These are not mentioned in the parallel place in Samuel; probably they did not arrive till the Ammonites and their other allies were defeated by the Israelites in the first battle.
entries.e3e444a685b0715dd097d3e13c0f5842ecefad65: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> Thirty and two thousand - The whole number mentioned in Samuel is, Syrians, of Beth-rehob, and of Zoba, twenty thousand; of King Maacah, one thousand; of Ish-tob, twelve thousand; in all thirty-three thousand. Of chariots or cavalry there is no mention. These could not have been the whole army.
entries.e3a231598e8aa99a5e95887203aa66e9207cff29: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen13697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13698" type="x-p"/> Be of good courage - See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.12">2Sam 10:12</reference>.
entries.93fe5055007bedd6a408eb80b59234b16a362011: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> Forty thousand footmen - See this number accounted for in the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.18">2Sam 10:18</reference> (note).
entries.d40aabfa8a7d109263aeefdc40312932d317aad7: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen13699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13700" type="x-p"/> They made peace with David, and became his servants - See on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.19">2Sam 10:19</reference> (note), and the concluding note in that place; and see for omissions in Chronicles, the preface to these books.  <chapter eID="1Chr.19"/> <div eID="gen13700" type="x-p"/>

entries.21ee15cdd35955d33ab60a2d20b2306599254713: <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1-1Chr.19.19">1Ch 19:1-19</reference> <div eID="gen5803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5804" type="x-p"/> The same phenomena are met with in the detailed account of the Ammonite-Syriac war, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1-1Chr.19.2">1Ch 19:1-2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference>, as compared with 2 Sam 10:1-11:1, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26">2Sa 12:26</reference>-31. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.1">1Ch 19:1</reference> the omission of the name הנוּן after בּנו is merely an oversight, as the omission of the name נחשׁ in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sa 10:1</reference></hi> also is. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.3">1Ch 19:3</reference> there is no need to alter וגו ולהפך לחקר into וגו וּלרגּלהּ את־העיר חקר, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sa 10:3</reference>, although the expression in Samuel is more precise. If the actual words of the original document are given in Samuel, the author of the Chronicle has made the thought more general: “to search and to overthrow, and to spy out the land.” Perhaps, however, the terms made use of in the original document were not so exact and precise as those of the book of Samuel. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.6">1Ch 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Ch 19:7</reference>, at least, the divergence from <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:16</reference> cannot be explained otherwise than by supposing that in neither of the narratives is the text of the original document exactly and perfectly reproduced. For a further discussion of the differences, see on 2Sa 10:6. The special statement as to the place where the mercenaries encamped, and the Ammonites gathered themselves together from out their cities (<reference osisRef="1Chr.19.7">1Ch 19:7</reference>), is wanting in 2nd Samuel. The city Medeba, which, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference>, was assigned to the tribe of Reuben, lay about two hours southeast from Heshbon, and still exists as ruins, which retain the ancient name Medaba (see on Num 21:30). In <reference osisRef="1Chr.19.9">1Ch 19:9</reference>, העיר פּתח, “outside the city” (i.e., the capital Rabbah), more correct or exact than השּׁער פּתח (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.8">2Sa 10:8</reference>). On אליהם ויּבא, as compared with חלאמה ויּבא (<reference osisRef="2Sam.10.17">2Sa 10:17</reference>), cf. the discussion on <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.16">2Sa 10:16</reference>-17.  <chapter eID="1Chr.19"/> <div eID="gen5804" type="x-p"/>

entries.0bdebeaa6b6af1e6c080f0b4055607b138920d6c:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="19" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XIX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Sam. 10. 1. &c.</ns0:note> it came to pass after this, that Nahash the king of the children of Ammon died <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of all the Contents of this Chapter see the Notes on 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 10. where we have the same things and almost the very same words.</ns0:note>, and his son reigned in his stead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And David said, I will shew kindness unto Ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nun the son of Nahash, because his father shewed kindness to me. And David sent messengers to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ort him concerning his father: so the servants of David came into the land of the children of Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon, to Hanun, to comfort him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 But the princes of the children of Ammon said to Hanun, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>in thine eyes doth Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> Thinkest thou that David doth honour thy father that he hath sent comforters unto thee? are not his servants come unto thee for to search, and to overthrow, and to spie out the land?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Wherefore Hanun took Davids servants, and shaved them, and cut off their Garments in the midst hard by their buttocks, and sent them away.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Then there went <ns0:hi>certain,</ns0:hi> and told David how the men were served. And he sent to meet them (for the men were greatly ashamed) and the king said, tarry at Jericho until your beards be grown, and <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> return.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And when the children of Ammon saw that they had made themselves <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> odious to David, Hanun and the children of Ammon sent a thousand talents of silver to hire them chariots and horsemen out of Mesopotamia, and out of Syria-maachah, and out of Zobah.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 So they hired thirty and two thousand chari<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ots <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> 32000 Men fighting from or with Chariots, as that word is elsewhere used: of which see my Notes on 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 5. And this Interpretation seems the more probable by comparing this place with 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 10. 6. where this Army is said to consist of 2000<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>footmen,</ns0:hi> and 12000 <ns0:hi>men of Ishtob;</ns0:hi> which make up these 32000 men, who fought partly from Chariots, and partly on Foot with Chariots or attending upon the Chariots, as the Ancient Manner of fighting was. And here <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6. this Army it made up of <ns0:hi>Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riots and Horsemen;</ns0:hi> where, except the <ns0:hi>chariots</ns0:hi> be understood, there were no Footmen in the Army, which is unusual and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />credible.</ns0:note>, and the king of Maachah and his people, who came and pitched before Medeba. And the children of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities, and came to battel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And when David heard <ns0:hi>of it,</ns0:hi> he sent Joab, and all the host of the mighty <ns0:hi>men.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And the children of Ammon came out, and put the battel in aray before the gate of the city: and the kings that were come, <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> by themselves in the field.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Now when Joab saw that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> the battel was set against him, before and behind, he chose out of all the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> choice of Israel, and put <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> in aray against the Assyrians.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And the rest of the people he delivered unto the hand of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> Abishai his brother, and they set them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in aray against the children of Ammon.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And he said, If the Syrians be too strong for me, then thou shalt help me: but if the children of Ammon be too strong for thee, then I will help thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 Be of good courage, and let us behave our selves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the LORD do <ns0:hi>that which is</ns0:hi> good in his sight.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 So Joab and the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> with him, drew nigh before the Syrians, unto the battel; and they fled before him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And when the children of Ammon saw that the Syrians were fled, they likewise fled before A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bishai his brother, and entred into the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And when the Syrians saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers and drew forth the Syrians that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> beyond the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> river: and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> Shophach, the captain of the host of Hada<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rezer, <ns0:hi>went</ns0:hi> before them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And it was told David, and he gathered all Israel, and passed over Jordan, and came upon them, and set <ns0:hi>the battel</ns0:hi> in aray against them, so when Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid had put the battel in aray against the Syrians, they fought with him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 But the Syrians fled before Israel, and David slew of the Syrians seven thousand men, <ns0:hi>which fought in</ns0:hi> chariots, and forty thousand footmen <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">How this agrees with 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 10. 18. see in the Notes on that place.</ns0:note>, and killed Shophach the captain of the host.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And when the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David, and became his servants: neither would the Syrians help the children of Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon any more.</ns0:p>
